overview.title: 📖 Overview: How Forbidden Things Are Destroyed
overview.subtitle: Temurah 34a–34b
overview.hebrewSource: זֶה הַכְּלָל: כׇּל הַנִּקְבָּרִין לֹא יִשָּׂרְפוּ, וְכׇל הַנִּשְׂרָפִין לֹא יִקָּבְרוּ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The mishna's two lists — buried and burned — end with a hard rule: the methods may not be exchanged. The reason is not ceremonial but practical: ash of a burned item may be used, ash of a buried item may not, so burning what should be buried risks a leniency down the line. Tavi then presses Rav Naḥman with a contradiction between this mishna and one in Orla about a nazirite's hair and a firstborn donkey's, drawing four separate answers from four Sages. The daf — and the tractate — closes on when the ash of consecrated property is permitted, and when it is barred forever.

slides.title: ✂️ Tavi's Contradiction: Buried Here, Burned There
slides.subtitle: Our mishna buries the nazirite's hair; Orla 3:3 burns the garment it was woven into

lines.speaker: Tavi
lines.text: Our mishna: the hair of a nazirite is buried. But Orla teaches that one who weaves a sit of firstborn wool, or a nazirite's hair, into a garment — the garment is burned!

lines.speaker: Rav Naḥman
lines.text: No contradiction. Ours is an impure nazirite, who shaves and starts afresh; Orla speaks of the pure nazirite who completes his term — his hair goes under the peace-offering pot.

lines.speaker: Tavi
lines.text: That settles nazirite against nazirite. But the firstborn donkey against firstborn donkey still stands — ours buries its hair, Orla burns it.

lines.speaker: Rav Sheshet
lines.text: (via Tavi, when Rav Naḥman fell silent) There, the hair was woven into a sack; here it is the hair itself.

lines.speaker: R' Yosei b. Ḥanina
lines.text: The same distinction — woven into a sack versus the hair on its own.

lines.speaker: R' Elazar
lines.text: And the same nazirite distinction as Rav Naḥman's — Orla means the pure nazirite, ours the impure one.

callout.label: Note:
callout.text: Rav Naḥman's silence on the donkey is preserved in the text — he asks Tavi whether he has heard an answer from others rather than supplying one.

slides.title: 🧵 Why Isn't the Forbidden Hair Simply Nullified?
slides.subtitle: Rav Naḥman presses Rav Sheshet on the woven-sack answer

nodes.content: ❓ If the hair is woven into a sack, let it be nullified by the majority of permitted material — why burn the sack at all?
💡 Rav Pappa: the case is where the forbidden hair was woven into an ornamental design of a bird — a significant item, and significant items are not nullified
❓ Then why burn the whole sack? Remove the bird designs and keep the rest!

columns.label: R' Yirmeya
columns.content: Orla follows Rabbi Yehuda, who permits burning what should be buried as a personal stringency

columns.label: Rav Naḥman's retort
columns.content: Even Rabbi Yehuda would not burn a sack he could simply repair — the objection was about removal, not stringency

nodes.content: ✅ R' Yirmeya clarifies: if removal is possible, fine — his answer is only a third resolution for where it is not

callout.label: Design as significance:
callout.text: A woven bird is treated as a thing in its own right rather than as scattered fibres, which is why the majority does not swallow it.

slides.title: 🔥 The Burning List, Clause by Clause
slides.subtitle: Whom does each ruling follow, and what does it mean in practice?
rows: An unattributed mishna following Rabbi Yehuda, who allows only burning; the Rabbis permit any form of destruction
One may even kindle a fire with its bread and oil, though the priest benefits
Foods are burned; liquids are buried — the method follows the substance
Provisional guilt offering, once he learns he did not sin
Treated as an unfit offering; Rabbi Yehuda says buried
Bird sin offering brought on uncertainty
It cannot be eaten, and its neck was pinched rather than slaughtered
Severed limb by limb and cast in, each limb carried out to the Kidron

callout.label: The governing rule:
callout.text: All that are buried shall not be burned, and all that are burned shall not be buried. Rabbi Yehuda permits burning as a stringency; the Rabbis refuse, since it could end in a leniency.

slides.title: 🪵 Are the Ashes Permitted?
slides.subtitle: The reason behind the no-swapping rule, and the sources that seem to contradict it

boxes.title: The rule's rationale
items: So burning what should be buried might lead one to use the ash

boxes.title: Two challenges
items: A corpse and menstrual blood that dried and crumbled are pure — so is buried matter's residue permitted? (Answered: pure of impurity, not permitted for benefit)
Rav Pineḥas: a bird burnt offering's crop and feathers leave the laws of me'ilah — yet they are buried

boxes.title: And the reverse challenge
items: A baraita: ashes of all burned prohibited items are permitted — except an ashera and consecrated property
Ashera and hekdesh taught separately because an ashera can be nullified by a gentile; hekdesh never can
So the ash of consecrated property is barred forever

callout.label: Two resolutions:
callout.text: Rami bar Ḥama: ash is permitted where the consecrated item was already disqualified, or where burning it incurred me'ilah — the misuse itself desanctifies it; the baraita speaks of a fire that fell by itself. Rav Shemaya: the baraita is about the daily removal of the ashes.

slides.title: 🌅 Terumat HaDeshen — The Ash That Stays Forbidden
slides.subtitle: Reading Leviticus 6:3 word by word

steps.content: 1️⃣ 'And he shall take up the ashes to which the fire has consumed the burnt offering on the altar, and he shall put them beside the altar'
2️⃣ 'And he shall put them' — he places them down gently, not casting them
3️⃣ 'them' — he puts down all of them, not a portion
4️⃣ The superfluous 'and' — he shall not scatter them
5️⃣ This is the case in which the ash of consecrated property is prohibited forever — the removed ashes rest beside the altar and are never put to use

callout.label: Closing the tractate:
callout.text: Temurah ends where it has been heading all along — on the precise fate of sanctity that can no longer serve its purpose, and on the care with which even its residue is handled.

summary.principle: Burial and burning are not interchangeable, because their ashes carry different law — and the tractate closes by mapping exactly when the residue of consecrated property may be used and when it is barred forever.

flowSteps.content: ✂️ Tavi's contradiction: nazirite's hair and firstborn donkey's hair — buried in our mishna, burned in Orla

columns.content: 🧑 Pure nazirite (burned) vs. impure nazirite (buried) — Rav Naḥman, R' Elazar
🧵 Woven into a sack (burned) vs. the hair itself (buried) — Rav Sheshet, R' Yosei b. Ḥanina

flowSteps.content: 🐦 Rav Pappa: a woven bird design is significant and not nullified; R' Yirmeya adds Rabbi Yehuda's stringency where removal is impossible
⚖️ Never swap the methods — ash of burned items is permitted, ash of buried items is not
🎓 Key Principle: consecrated ash is permitted once the item was disqualified or misused, but the ashes removed from the altar each morning stay forbidden forever

quiz.q: How does Rav Naḥman resolve the contradiction about the nazirite's hair?
o: Orla speaks of an impure nazirite, our mishna of a pure one
Our mishna speaks of an impure nazirite who shaves and starts anew; Orla speaks of a pure nazirite completing his term
The hair is always burned, and our mishna is a minority view
Both mishnayot speak of a firstborn donkey, not a nazirite
quiz.e: The pure nazirite's hair goes under the pot of his peace offering and is burned; the impure nazirite's shorn hair is buried. Rabbi Elazar gives the same answer.

quiz.q: Why is the forbidden hair woven into a sack not nullified by the majority?
o: Because hair is never nullified
Because Rav Pappa explains it was woven into an ornamental bird design, which is significant in its own right
Because the sack was consecrated
Because a sit is a large enough quantity to matter
quiz.e: Rav Naḥman raises the nullification objection, and Rav Pappa answers that a woven design counts as a distinct significant item, which the surrounding majority does not absorb.

quiz.q: What is the Rabbis' reason for forbidding one to burn an item that should be buried?
o: Burning is a more severe form of destruction
Because the ash of a burned item is permitted while the ash of a buried item is not, so it could lead to a leniency
Because only priests may burn consecrated items
Because burial preserves the item's sanctity
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda permits the swap as a personal stringency, but the Rabbis point out that it converts forbidden ash into ash people will treat as permitted.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Yehuda hold that an uncertain bird sin offering is disposed of?
o: It is burned like an unfit offering
It is buried whole
It is severed limb by limb and cast into the Temple courtyard drain, washing out to the Kidron
It is given to the priests of the serving watch
quiz.e: The baraita spells out his method: dismembering the bird and casting the limbs into the drain, where the liquids carry each limb out.

quiz.q: According to Rav Shemaya, which case is the baraita describing when it says the ash of consecrated property is prohibited forever?
o: Any offering that was burned after disqualification
The daily removal of the ashes from the altar (terumat hadeshen)
Wood of an ashera that was burned
Ash of impure teruma used to kindle a fire
quiz.e: Rav Shemaya restricts the baraita to terumat hadeshen, the morning rite in which ashes are placed beside the altar — and Leviticus 6:3 is expounded to require placing them gently, all of them, without scattering.
